[[gfx-buffers|El shader que recuerda]] y: [[gfx-buffers|The shader that remembers]] already computed each frame from the previous one. This topic sets it to moving ink and smoke: [[av-vectorial|divergence and curl]], the Laplacian of the [[av-edp|heat equation]] and [[gfx-ruido|noise]] are all reused, and the noise here turns into a field of currents.
El humo de una vela, la leche que se abr: The smoke of a candle, the milk opening out in the coffee, the ink in the water: everything that flows obeys some nineteenth-century equations that are still not fully solved. But to draw it you do not need to solve them exactly. Three ideas that fit in a shader with memory are enough: transporting what is there by looking backwards, moving things with a field that creates no gaps, and letting the fluid push itself.
Un fluido lleva cosas consigo: tinta, ca: A fluid carries things with it: ink, heat, its own velocity. That transport is called advection. If at each pixel there is a velocity $\vec v$, the ink that will be at a point an instant from now is the ink that is now a little further back, exactly at the place the current brings it from:
c(\\vec x,\\ t + \\Delta t) = c(\\vec x: c(\vec x,\ t + \Delta t) = c(\vec x - \vec v\,\Delta t,\ t)
Se dice: <em>«la tinta en x dentro de un:
It reads: “the ink at x an instant from now is the ink that is now at x minus v times delta t”. In the shader, with the velocity in pixels per step: texture2D(iChannel0, (fragCoord - v * dt) / iResolution.xy).

It is called semi-Lagrangian because it follows the fluid particle (Lagrange's point of view) for one step only, and then returns to the fixed grid (Euler's).
Lo natural sería lo contrario: coger la: The natural thing would be the opposite: take each pixel's ink and push it towards where it is going. In a shader that is impossible, because each pixel writes only its own colour. And looking backwards has another enormous virtue: the texture interpolates between pixels, and an interpolation never gives a value larger than the largest or smaller than the smallest. However large the velocity is, the method does not go out of control, unlike the explicit heat method of [[gfx-buffers]]. The price is that it blurs a little at each step.
Un visor con memoria transporta tinta co: A viewer with memory transports ink with velocity $\vec v$, in pixels per step. Where does the pixel $(120, 80)$ read from with $\vec v = (3, -2)$? And with $\vec v = (2{.}5,\ 0)$, if in row 80 the ink is $0{.}8$ at column 117 and $0{.}2$ at column 118?
<strong>Mirar atrás.</strong> $(120, 80): Looking back. $(120, 80) - (3, -2) = (117, 82)$: three pixels to the left and two upwards. The current goes to the right and downwards, so what arrives here came from there.
¿Se suma o se resta la velocidad?: Is the velocity added or subtracted?
<strong>Entre dos píxeles.</strong> Con: Between two pixels. With $\vec v = (2{.}5,\ 0)$ you read at $(117{.}5,\ 80)$, halfway between columns 117 and 118. The texture interpolates: $0{.}5\cdot 0{.}8 + 0{.}5\cdot 0{.}2 = 0{.}5$.
¿Qué devuelve <code>texture2D</code> al: What does texture2D return when reading between two pixels?
<strong>El precio.</strong> Un borde que: The price. An edge that was $0{.}8$ next to $0{.}2$ has become a $0{.}5$. Every step with a non-integer displacement averages neighbours: it is numerical diffusion, and that is why the ink blurs over time even if the fluid has no viscosity.
<strong>La garantía.</strong> Ese $0{,}5: The guarantee. That $0{.}5$ lies between $0{.}2$ and $0{.}8$. An interpolation invents no values outside those that were already there: looking backwards, the ink cannot grow out of control, whatever happens to the velocity.
Jos Stam presentó este método en 1999 co: Jos Stam presented this method in 1999 under the name “stable fluids”, precisely because of that guarantee, and it is the basis of many real-time smoke simulators.
¿Por qué la advección se programa mirand: Why is advection programmed by looking backwards and not by pushing the ink forwards?
Porque cada píxel solo escribe su propio: Because each pixel writes only its own colour: it knows where to read from, but it cannot write anywhere else
Empujar hacia delante obligaría a escrib: Pushing forwards would mean writing into the destination pixel, and besides, two pixels could send their ink to the same place and leave another empty. Looking backwards, each pixel receives exactly one value.
Porque así el fluido va más deprisa: Because that way the fluid goes faster
La velocidad es la misma en los dos caso: The velocity is the same in both cases. What changes is how it is computed, and the backwards version is the only one that fits in a fragment shader.
Se podría repartir la tinta entre varios: You could share the ink out among several destination pixels. The problem is that a fragment shader cannot write into any pixel but its own.
Un campo sin huecos: ruido rizado: A field with no gaps: curl noise
Para transportar hace falta una velocida: To transport you need a velocity at each point: a vector field. But not just any one will do. Water and slow smoke are almost incompressible: what enters a region comes out again. That is asking the field to have zero [[av-vectorial|divergence]], and with just any field it does not happen: the ink would pile up in some places and leave gaps in others.
Hay un truco que da campos sin divergenc: There is a trick that gives divergence-free fields for free. You take any function $\psi$ of the plane, the stream function, and instead of its gradient you use the gradient rotated by 90°:
\\vec v = \\left(\\frac{\\partial \\psi}: \vec v = \left(\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial y},\ -\frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}\right)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \nabla\cdot\vec v = \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial x\,\partial y} - \frac{\partial^2 \psi}{\partial y\,\partial x} = 0
el rotacional de una función de corrient: the curl of a stream function
Las dos derivadas cruzadas son iguales,:
The two cross derivatives are equal, so they cancel: the divergence is zero whatever $\psi$ is.

Besides, the gradient is perpendicular to the level curves, and rotated by 90° it is tangent to them: the fluid circulates along the level curves of $\psi$, which are the streamlines. If $\psi$ is a [[gfx-ruido|noise]], out come currents and swirls: this is called curl noise.

In a real fluid, the velocity also transports itself —a swirl goes on turning even if nobody stirs it— and it changes for three further reasons: pressure pushes from where the fluid piles up towards where it is scarce, viscosity evens out each point's velocity with its neighbours', and outside forces, like a jet, add movement. They are the Navier-Stokes equations.

La primera es la <strong>continuidad</st:
The first is continuity: the density $\rho$ falls where the flow diverges and rises where it converges. The second says how the velocity changes, term by term: it transports itself, the pressure, proportional to the density's gradient, pushes downhill, the Laplacian $\Delta\vec v$ smooths it like heat, with viscosity $\nu$, and $\vec f$ is the outside forces.

A genuinely incompressible fluid would require solving a Poisson equation at each step, with many passes. Guay, Colin and Egli's trick is to leave it slightly compressible: where density accumulates, the pressure sends it back. It all fits in a single pass per pixel.

Cada nube de humo, explosión, ola y cabe: Every cloud of smoke, explosion, wave and head of hair that moves in an animated film comes out of a fluid simulator, and the real-time ones in video games almost always use this topic's backward advection. But the most serious application is not visual: weather forecasting models transport temperature, humidity and wind over a grid of the planet every day with semi-Lagrangian schemes, because they allow long time steps without the computation going out of control. And curl noise is used to move smoke and snow particles without simulating anything.
Claude-Louis Navier escribió en 1822 las: Claude-Louis Navier wrote down the equations of a viscous fluid's motion in 1822, and George Stokes redid them more carefully in 1845. In 2000 the Clay Institute included them among its seven Millennium Problems: it is still not known whether, in three dimensions, their solutions can blow up in finite time, and whoever solves it will collect a million dollars. Meanwhile, Jos Stam presented his stable fluids for the cinema in 1999, Robert Bridson published curl noise in 2007, and Martin Guay, Fabrice Colin and Richard Egli described in 2011 the single-pass fluid this topic uses.
